claim: Vrl1 and VARP share a VPS9 domain, a conserved N-terminus, and an ankyrin repeat domain (AnkRD) that are not found in other yeast VPS9-domain GEFs.
source: Vrl1 and its human ortholog VARP share a VPS9 domain, as well as a conserved N-terminus and ankyrin repeat domain (AnkRD) that are not found in other yeast VPS9-domain GEFs (Herman et al., 2018; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Herman et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 1A showing domain architecture.

claim: Vrl1 features a ~350 amino acid unannotated region downstream of the AnkRD that is not present in VARP.
source: Vrl1 also features a ~350 amino acid (aa) unannotated region downstream of the AnkRD that is not present in VARP.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis comparing Vrl1 and VARP domain structures.

claim: The protein fold recognition program Phyre2 identified a PX-BAR module in Vrl1 with 98.6% confidence in the region aa 737–1089.
source: The protein fold recognition program Phyre2 (Kelley et al., 2015) identified a PX-BAR module with very high confidence (98.6%) in this region (aa 737–1089; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by computational prediction using Phyre2 software and shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Ab initio modeling of the Vrl1 region aa 737-1089 by AlphaFold2-powered ColabFold software predicted a structure with striking similarity to the PX-BAR fold.
source: ab initio modeling of this region by AlphaFold2-powered ColabFold software (Mirdita et al., 2022) predicted a structure with striking similarity to the PX-BAR fold (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational structure prediction using ColabFold and shown in figures.

claim: The predicted Vrl1 PX domain is missing key residues for PI3P binding.
source: Because the predicted Vrl1 PX domain is missing key residues for PI3P binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), we refer to it as a 'PX-like' domain.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Vrl1 is the first VPS9 domain-containing protein with predicted structural homology to the SNX-BAR family.
source: To our knowledge, Vrl1 is the first VPS9 domain-containing protein with predicted structural homology to the SNX-BAR family.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and their structural predictions.

claim: Vrl1-Envy colocalizes with Did2-mRuby2-labeled endosomes at 56%.
source: We found that Vrl1, when C-terminally tagged with the bright GFP variant Envy, was present at perivacuolar puncta that colocalize with the endosomal marker Did2-mRuby2, but not the Golgi protein Sec7-dsRed (56% and 2%, respectively, p<0.0001; Figure 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization data shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: Vrl1-Envy colocalizes with Sec7-dsRed Golgi marker at 2%.
source: We found that Vrl1, when C-terminally tagged with the bright GFP variant Envy, was present at perivacuolar puncta that colocalize with the endosomal marker Did2-mRuby2, but not the Golgi protein Sec7-dsRed (56% and 2%, respectively, p<0.0001; Figure 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization data shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: Unlike other yeast VPS9-domain GEFs, Vrl1 constitutively localizes to endosomes.
source: These observations indicate that unlike other yeast VPS9-domain GEFs (Paulsel et al., 2013), Vrl1 constitutively localizes to endosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on the colocalization data and comparison to literature on other VPS9-domain GEFs.

claim: A DHFR proximity screen identified the endosomal Rab GTPases Vps21 (Z=18.7) and Ypt52 (Z=7.6) as Vrl1 interactors.
source: This identified the endosomal Rab GTPases Vps21 (Z=18.7) and Ypt52 (Z=7.6), and other conserved endosomal proteins including the retromer subunit Vps35 (Z=13), the hydrolase receptors Vps10 (Z=12.9) and Mrl1 (Z=7.7), and components of the Class C Core complex Vps11 (Z=16.9) and Vps18 (Z=12.2; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by DHFR screen data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The DHFR screen identified the retromer subunit Vps35 (Z=13) as a Vrl1 interactor.
source: This identified the endosomal Rab GTPases Vps21 (Z=18.7) and Ypt52 (Z=7.6), and other conserved endosomal proteins including the retromer subunit Vps35 (Z=13), the hydrolase receptors Vps10 (Z=12.9) and Mrl1 (Z=7.7), and components of the Class C Core complex Vps11 (Z=16.9) and Vps18 (Z=12.2; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by DHFR screen data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The DHFR screen identified the hydrolase receptors Vps10 (Z=12.9) and Mrl1 (Z=7.7) as Vrl1 interactors.
source: This identified the endosomal Rab GTPases Vps21 (Z=18.7) and Ypt52 (Z=7.6), and other conserved endosomal proteins including the retromer subunit Vps35 (Z=13), the hydrolase receptors Vps10 (Z=12.9) and Mrl1 (Z=7.7), and components of the Class C Core complex Vps11 (Z=16.9) and Vps18 (Z=12.2; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by DHFR screen data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The DHFR screen identified components of the Class C Core complex Vps11 (Z=16.9) and Vps18 (Z=12.2) as Vrl1 interactors.
source: This identified the endosomal Rab GTPases Vps21 (Z=18.7) and Ypt52 (Z=7.6), and other conserved endosomal proteins including the retromer subunit Vps35 (Z=13), the hydrolase receptors Vps10 (Z=12.9) and Mrl1 (Z=7.7), and components of the Class C Core complex Vps11 (Z=16.9) and Vps18 (Z=12.2; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by DHFR screen data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Functional enrichment analysis of Vrl1 interactors (Z>2) highlighted relationships with retromer and the CORVET complex.
source: Functional enrichment analysis of Vrl1 interactors (Z>2) highlighted relationships with other subunits of endosomal complexes including retromer and the CORVET complex (Figure 1G, Supplementary file 2; Ashburner et al., 2000; Gene Ontology Consortium, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The DHFR screen identified a strong connection between Vrl1 and the uncharacterized SNX-BAR Ykr078w (Z=9.5).
source: Our DHFR screen identified a strong connection between Vrl1 and the uncharacterized SNX-BAR Ykr078w (Z=9.5), the paralog of membrane-binding retromer subunit Vps5 (Byrne and Wolfe, 2005; Horazdovsky et al., 1997), which we have named 'Vrl1-Interacting Sorting Nexin 1' or Vin1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DHFR screen data and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Ykr078w is the paralog of membrane-binding retromer subunit Vps5.
source: Our DHFR screen identified a strong connection between Vrl1 and the uncharacterized SNX-BAR Ykr078w (Z=9.5), the paralog of membrane-binding retromer subunit Vps5 (Byrne and Wolfe, 2005; Horazdovsky et al., 1997), which we have named 'Vrl1-Interacting Sorting Nexin 1' or Vin1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Byrne and Wolfe, 2005 and Horazdovsky et al., 1997.

claim: Vin1 has a reported cytosolic distribution.
source: Vin1 has a reported cytosolic distribution (Huh et al., 2003), which is surprising given that its paralog Vps5 localizes to endosomes in a PI3P-dependent manner (Burda et al., 2002) and that Vin1 interacts with PI3P in vitro (Yu and Lemmon, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Huh et al., 2003.

claim: Vps5 localizes to endosomes in a PI3P-dependent manner.
source: Vin1 has a reported cytosolic distribution (Huh et al., 2003), which is surprising given that its paralog Vps5 localizes to endosomes in a PI3P-dependent manner (Burda et al., 2002) and that Vin1 interacts with PI3P in vitro (Yu and Lemmon, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Burda et al., 2002.

claim: Vin1 interacts with PI3P in vitro.
source: Vin1 has a reported cytosolic distribution (Huh et al., 2003), which is surprising given that its paralog Vps5 localizes to endosomes in a PI3P-dependent manner (Burda et al., 2002) and that Vin1 interacts with PI3P in vitro (Yu and Lemmon, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yu and Lemmon, 2001.

claim: Increasing Vin1 levels did not alter its cytosolic distribution pattern in endogenously expressed N- and C-terminally tagged strains.
source: Increasing Vin1 levels did not alter its cytosolic distribution pattern which we observed in both endogenously expressed N- and C-terminally tagged strains (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of VRL1 caused a dramatic redistribution of Vin1-Envy from the cytosol to intracellular puncta (p<0.0001).
source: Indeed, we found that expression of VRL1 caused a dramatic redistribution of Vin1-Envy from the cytosol to intracellular puncta (p<0.0001; Figure 2B, C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: Over-expressing VRL1 from the ADH1pr further increased the number of bright Vin1-Envy puncta (p<0.0001).
source: and that over-expressing VRL1 from the ADH1pr further increased the number of bright Vin1-Envy puncta (p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Deletion of VIN1 prevented Vrl1-Envy from forming intracellular puncta (p<0.001).
source: Deletion of VIN1 prevented Vrl1-Envy from forming intracellular puncta (p<0.001; Figure 2B, C)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: The localization of Vrl1 and Vin1 is highly interdependent.
source: suggesting that the localization of Vrl1 and Vin1 is highly interdependent.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mutual dependence of Vrl1 and Vin1 for punctate localization.

claim: The levels of triple hemagglutinin (3HA)-tagged Vrl1 were reduced to 17% of WT (p<0.001) in strains lacking VIN1.
source: Vrl1 and Vin1 are also dependent on each other for stability, as the levels of triple hemagglutinin (3HA)-tagged Vrl1 and Vin1 were severely reduced in strains lacking VIN1 or VRL1 (17% of WT, p<0.001 and 18% of WT, p<0.01, respectively; Figure 2D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: The levels of triple hemagglutinin (3HA)-tagged Vin1 were reduced to 18% of WT (p<0.01) in strains lacking VRL1.
source: Vrl1 and Vin1 are also dependent on each other for stability, as the levels of triple hemagglutinin (3HA)-tagged Vrl1 and Vin1 were severely reduced in strains lacking VIN1 or VRL1 (17% of WT, p<0.001 and 18% of WT, p<0.01, respectively; Figure 2D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: Vin1-3HA strongly co-purified with Vrl1-Envy (64% recovery of Vin1).
source: We found that Vin1-3HA strongly co-purified with Vrl1-Envy (64% recovery of Vin1; Figure 2F)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Vrl1-Envy and Vin1-mScarletI showed a high degree of colocalization at endosomal puncta (88%).
source: and Vrl1-Envy and Vin1-mScarletI (-mScI) showed a high degree of colocalization at endosomal puncta (88%; Figure 2G)
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Vrl1 was displaced to the cytosol in a PI3K deletion mutant (vps34Δ, p<0.01).
source: Vrl1 was displaced to the cytosol in a PI3K deletion mutant (vps34Δ, p<0.01; Figure 2H, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 2H, I.

claim: The PX domain of Vin1 is important for endosomal recruitment.
source: Since the Vrl1 PX domain is missing residues that are typically required to bind PI3P, this suggests the PX domain of Vin1 is important for endosomal recruitment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Vrl1 requires PI3P for localization but lacks PI3P-binding residues.

claim: Vin1 binds to PI3P through an unconventional motif in its PX domain.
source: Indeed, a recent study demonstrated that Vin1, therein referred to as Vps501, binds to PI3P through an unconventional motif in its PX domain (Goyal et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Goyal et al., 2022.

claim: In a muk1Δvps9Δ strain lacking all other VPS9-domain GEFs, Vrl1 localization is dependent on a conserved catalytic residue in the VPS9 domain (Vrl1D373; p<0.001).
source: We found that, in a muk1Δvps9Δ strain that lacks all other VPS9-domain GEFs, Vrl1 localization is dependent on a conserved catalytic residue in the VPS9 domain (Vrl1D373; Bean et al., 2015; p<0.001; Figure 2J, K)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 2J, K, and citation to Bean et al., 2015.

claim: Vrl1 may leverage its ability to stimulate endosomal PI3P production and promote its own membrane recruitment.
source: suggesting that Vrl1 may leverage its ability to stimulate endosomal PI3P production and promote its own membrane recruitment.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the dependence of Vrl1 localization on its GEF activity.

claim: Vrl1 and Vin1 form a novel complex that localizes to endosomes in a PI3P-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that Vrl1 and Vin1 form a novel complex that localizes to endosomes in a PI3P-dependent manner (Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Neither Vrl1 nor Vin1 is stable or capable of membrane localization in the absence of the other.
source: Since neither Vrl1 nor Vin1 is stable or capable of membrane localization in the absence of the other, we reason that these proteins primarily exist as members of this complex which we have named the 'VPS9 GEF-Interacting Sorting Nexin' or VINE complex.
evidence: The claim is based on the stability and localization data presented earlier.

claim: ColabFold software predicted that the PX-like and BAR domains of Vrl1 (aa 732–1090) bind to the PX and BAR domains of Vin1 (aa 110–585) to form a canonical SNX-BAR dimer (pTMscore = 0.75).
source: ColabFold software (Mirdita et al., 2022) predicted that the PX-like and BAR domains of Vrl1 (aa 732–1090) bind to the PX and BAR domains of Vin1 (aa 110–585) to form a canonical SNX-BAR dimer (pTMscore = 0.75; Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational structure prediction shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ColabFold accurately predicted the homodimerization of Mvp1.
source: This accurately predicted the homodimerization of Mvp1 (Suzuki et al., 2021) and the heterodimerization of Vps5/Vps17 (Seaman and Williams, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of predictions to known interactions from literature.

claim: ColabFold accurately predicted the heterodimerization of Vps5/Vps17.
source: This accurately predicted the homodimerization of Mvp1 (Suzuki et al., 2021) and the heterodimerization of Vps5/Vps17 (Seaman and Williams, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of predictions to known interactions from literature.

claim: Neither Vrl1 nor Vin1 was predicted to form homodimers.
source: Neither Vrl1 nor Vin1 was predicted to form homodimers, although unexpectedly Vrl1 was predicted to pair equally well with both Vin1 and its paralog Vps5.
evidence: The claim is based on ColabFold predictions shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Vrl1 was predicted to pair equally well with both Vin1 and its paralog Vps5.
source: Neither Vrl1 nor Vin1 was predicted to form homodimers, although unexpectedly Vrl1 was predicted to pair equally well with both Vin1 and its paralog Vps5.
evidence: The claim is based on ColabFold predictions shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Vrl1 and Vps5 exhibit high confidence interactions with Vin1 and Vps17, respectively, whereas Vrl1 and Vps17 were predicted not to interact.
source: By comparing plots of predicted alignment error (PAE) for different combinations of SNX-BARs, we found that Vrl1 and Vps5 exhibit high confidence interactions with Vin1 and Vps17, respectively, whereas Vrl1 and Vps17 were predicted not to interact (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on PAE plot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Vin1 is the only yeast SNX-BAR that interacts with over-expressed Vrl1-3HA by CoIP.
source: First, we tested all known yeast SNX-BAR proteins for their ability to bind Vrl1 and found that Vin1 alone interacts with Vrl1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Vrl1 failed to bind Vps5 when VIN1 was deleted from a strain that over-expresses Vrl1.
source: Vrl1 also failed to bind Vps5 when VIN1 was deleted from a strain that over-expresses Vrl1 to compensate for its instability in the vin1∆ mutant (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Vrl1 did not interact with any of the other retromer subunits.
source: Further, Vrl1 did not interact with any of the other retromer subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Vrl1 was unable to promote the endosomal localization of Vps10 in strains lacking Vps5 and/or Vps17.
source: Using functional readouts, we found that Vrl1 was unable to promote the endosomal localization of Vps10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) or Vps35 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D) in strains lacking Vps5 and/or Vps17
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Vrl1 was unable to promote the endosomal localization of Vps35 in strains lacking Vps5 and/or Vps17.
source: Using functional readouts, we found that Vrl1 was unable to promote the endosomal localization of Vps10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) or Vps35 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D) in strains lacking Vps5 and/or Vps17
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C, D.

claim: Vrl1 does not functionally pair with retromer SNX-BARs.
source: indicating that Vrl1 does not functionally pair with retromer SNX-BARs and that Vin1/Vrl1 cannot replace Vps5/17 to form a retromer-like complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional assays showing Vrl1 cannot rescue retromer functions.

claim: Vin1/Vrl1 cannot replace Vps5/17 to form a retromer-like complex.
source: indicating that Vrl1 does not functionally pair with retromer SNX-BARs and that Vin1/Vrl1 cannot replace Vps5/17 to form a retromer-like complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional assays showing Vrl1 cannot rescue retromer functions.

claim: Vrl1 has strong paralog specificity.
source: These results further suggest that Vrl1 has strong paralog specificity and that interactions beyond the BAR-BAR interface could be responsible for its specific recognition of Vin1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the selective interaction of Vrl1 with Vin1 but not Vps5.

claim: Interactions beyond the BAR-BAR interface could be responsible for Vrl1's specific recognition of Vin1.
source: These results further suggest that Vrl1 has strong paralog specificity and that interactions beyond the BAR-BAR interface could be responsible for its specific recognition of Vin1.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the observed specificity.

claim: The GEF-deficient mutant (Vrl1D373A) significantly recruited Vin1 (p<0.0001).
source: We found that the GEF-deficient mutant (Vrl1D373A; Bean et al., 2015) and the N-terminal truncation (Vrl1158-end) significantly recruited Vin1 (p<0.0001 and p<0.001, respectively; Figure 3G)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 3F, G.

claim: The N-terminal truncation (Vrl1158-end) significantly recruited Vin1 (p<0.001).
source: We found that the GEF-deficient mutant (Vrl1D373A; Bean et al., 2015) and the N-terminal truncation (Vrl1158-end) significantly recruited Vin1 (p<0.0001 and p<0.001, respectively; Figure 3G)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 3F, G.

claim: Deletion of C-terminal sequences (i.e. Vrl11-465) blocked the membrane localization of both Vrl1 and Vin1.
source: Deletion of C-terminal sequences (i.e. Vrl11-465) blocked the membrane localization of both Vrl1 and Vin1.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The Vrl1(1-703)YPE chimera strongly recruited Vin1 to puncta (P<0.0001).
source: Strikingly, the resulting Vrl1(1-703)YPE chimera strongly recruited Vin1 to puncta (P<0.0001; Figure 3G)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 3F, G.

claim: BAR-BAR interactions are dispensable for Vin1 recruitment.
source: suggesting that BAR-BAR interactions are dispensable for Vin1 recruitment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Vrl1(1-703)YPE lacking BAR domain still recruits Vin1.

claim: The Vrl1(1-465)YPE construct localized to endosomes yet failed to recruit Vin1.
source: A further truncation that removed the AnkRD to create Vrl1(1-465)YPE localized to endosomes yet failed to recruit Vin1 (Figure 3F, G)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3F, G.

claim: The AnkRD contains a potent interacting interface for Vin1.
source: indicating that the AnkRD contains a potent interacting interface for Vin1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the loss of Vin1 recruitment when AnkRD is removed.

claim: The Vrl1465-end fragment which contains the AnkRD, PX-like and BAR domains weakly localized and recruited a small but significant amount of Vin1 (p<0.05).
source: In support of this idea, the Vrl1465-end fragment which contains the AnkRD, PX-like and BAR domains weakly localized and recruited a small but significant amount of Vin1 (p<0.05) while the Vrl1700-end fragment containing only the PX-like and BAR domains did not localize or recruit Vin1 (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 3F, G.

claim: The Vrl1700-end fragment containing only the PX-like and BAR domains did not localize or recruit Vin1.
source: In support of this idea, the Vrl1465-end fragment which contains the AnkRD, PX-like and BAR domains weakly localized and recruited a small but significant amount of Vin1 (p<0.05) while the Vrl1700-end fragment containing only the PX-like and BAR domains did not localize or recruit Vin1 (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3F, G.

claim: The VINE complex assembles primarily through an interaction between Vin1 and the Vrl1 AnkRD.
source: Taken together, the Vin1 recruitment assays, CoIPs and structural predictions suggest that the VINE complex assembles primarily through an interaction between Vin1 and the Vrl1 AnkRD, while a secondary interaction between the Vin1 and Vrl1 BAR domains may occur at the endosomal membrane.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from multiple experimental observations.

claim: A secondary interaction between the Vin1 and Vrl1 BAR domains may occur at the endosomal membrane.
source: Taken together, the Vin1 recruitment assays, CoIPs and structural predictions suggest that the VINE complex assembles primarily through an interaction between Vin1 and the Vrl1 AnkRD, while a secondary interaction between the Vin1 and Vrl1 BAR domains may occur at the endosomal membrane.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on structural predictions and experimental data.

claim: Vin1 and Vps5 have unstructured N-terminal regions preceding their respective PX domains (Vin11-116 and Vps51-276).
source: Vin1 and Vps5 have unstructured N-terminal regions preceding their respective PX domains (Vin11-116 and Vps51-276; Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Vrl1(1-703)YPE chimera showed strong recruitment of the Vin1 N-terminus, but not the YPE module alone (p<0.0001).
source: we observed strong recruitment of the Vin1 N-terminus by the Vrl1(1-703)YPE chimera, but not the YPE module alone (p<0.0001; Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: No recruitment of the Vps5 N-terminus was detected by any of the tested constructs.
source: In contrast, we detected no recruitment of the Vps5 N-terminus by any of our tested constructs
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The N-terminal regions of the paralogous SNX-BARs dictate specificity for Vrl1.
source: suggesting that the N-terminal regions of the paralogous SNX-BARs dictate specificity for Vrl1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential recruitment of Vin1 vs Vps5 N-termini.

claim: WT Vrl1-Envy recruited WT Vin1-mScI to colocalizing puncta.
source: We noticed that wild type (WT) Vrl1-Envy recruited WT Vin1-mScI to colocalizing puncta (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: WT Vrl1 was unable to recruit the Vin1 N-terminus.
source: but was unable to recruit the Vin1 N-terminus.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: WT Vrl1 failed to localize when the Vin1 N-terminus was expressed in a vin1∆ strain.
source: however this could not be tested directly because WT Vrl1 failed to localize when the Vin1 N-terminus was expressed in a vin1∆ strain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The Vin1 PX and BAR domains also contribute to VINE assembly and membrane recruitment.
source: This observation indicates that the Vin1 PX and BAR domains also contribute to VINE assembly and membrane recruitment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the inability of the Vin1 N-terminus alone to support Vrl1 localization.

claim: Only region 3 (Vin1 aa 76–95) was recruited to puncta by Vrl1(1-703)YPE in a vin1Δ strain (p<0.05).
source: When each of these fragments was fused to mScarletI (Figure 4F), only region 3 (Vin1 aa 76–95) was recruited to puncta by Vrl1(1-703)YPE in a vin1Δ strain (p<0.05; Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 4F, G.

claim: The Vrl1 AnkRD distinguishes Vin1 from Vps5 through a short sequence in the unstructured Vin1 N-terminus.
source: This suggests that the Vrl1 AnkRD distinguishes Vin1 from Vps5 through a short sequence in the unstructured Vin1 N-terminus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the recruitment of Vin1 region 3 but not Vps5 N-terminus.

claim: ColabFold confidently predicted an interaction between Vrl1(1-703) and the minimal Vin1 fragment (Vin176-95).
source: ColabFold confidently predicted an interaction between Vrl1(1-703) and the minimal Vin1 fragment (Vin176-95; Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational structure prediction shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: In the ColabFold model, Vin176-95 binds Vrl1 at an interface between the VPS9 domain and AnkRD that is conserved in the Saccharomycetaceae family.
source: In this model, Vin176-95 binds Vrl1 at an interface between the VPS9 domain and AnkRD that is conserved in the Saccharomycetaceae family (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the predicted structure and conservation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The exact Vin176-95 region identified in subcellular recruitment assays was the only sequence predicted to associate with Vrl1.
source: we performed a prediction with the entire Vin1 N-terminal sequence and found that the exact Vin176-95 region that we identified in our subcellular recruitment assay (Figure 4F, G) was the only sequence predicted to associate with Vrl1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ColabFold predictions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The Vin176-95 fragment contains a run of consecutive basic residues.
source: The Vin176-95 fragment contains a run of consecutive basic residues (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Acidic and polar residues in the corresponding Vrl1 AnkRD interface were among the most conserved within Saccharomycetaceae.
source: Interestingly, acidic and polar residues in the corresponding Vrl1 AnkRD interface were among the most conserved within Saccharomycetaceae (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: When five conserved acidic and polar residues were simultaneously substituted with alanine (EEDNE-5A), recruitment of the Vin1 N-terminus was lost (p<0.0001).
source: When five of the conserved acidic and polar residues were simultaneously substituted with alanine (EEDNE-5A), recruitment of the Vin1 N-terminus was lost (p<0.0001; Figure 5E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 5E, F.

claim: Swapping the charges of E510 resulted in complete loss of recruitment (p<0.0001).
source: In addition, swapping the charges of either E510 or D511 resulted in either complete or severe loss of recruitment, respectively (p<0.0001; Figure 5E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 5E, F.

claim: Swapping the charges of D511 resulted in severe loss of recruitment (p<0.0001).

claim: Vrl1 binds the Vin1 N-terminus through electrostatic interactions.

claim: VINE promotes the synthesis of endosomal PI3P only when fully assembled.

claim: Vrl1(1-465)YPE and Vrl1(1-703)YPE, but not WT Vrl1, fully rescued the endosomal localization of Vps26-mScarletI in a muk1Δvps9Δvin1∆ strain (p<0.001).

claim: Vin1 regulates the activity of Vrl1 by promoting its localization to endosomes.
source: These results suggest that Vin1 regulates the activity of Vrl1 by promoting its localization to endosomes.

claim: GFP-Vin1 was observed on tubular structures that eventually underwent scission and separated from the endosome.

claim: VRL1 expression had no significant effect on the localization of the retromer cargo Vps10.

claim: VRL1 expression had no significant effect on the localization of the Snx4 cargo Atg27.

claim: VRL1 expression caused a significant decrease in the number of bright Mrl1-GFP puncta per cell (61% decrease relative to vrl1, p<0.05).

claim: The bright Mrl1 puncta in vrl1 cells do not colocalize with the vacuolar marker GFP-Ypt7 (9.6%).
source: The bright Mrl1 puncta in vrl1 cells colocalize with the endosomal markers Did2-Envy and GFP-Vps21 (69% and 48%, respectively), but not with the vacuolar marker GFP-Ypt7 (9.6%, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Vrl1 redistributes Mrl1 from endosomes.
source: suggesting that Vrl1 redistributes Mrl1 from endosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the colocalization data showing Mrl1 at endosomes in vrl1 cells.

claim: Vrl1 GEF activity was not required for the redistribution of Mrl1 (p<0.05).
source: Vrl1 GEF activity was not required for this effect (p<0.05; Figure 7E, F)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 7E, F.

source: indicating that Vrl1 does not alter Mrl1 distribution by influencing the local activity of endosomal Rabs.

claim: Correction of the vrl1 frameshift mutation caused a similar change in Mrl1 localization (p<0.01).

claim: The VINE complex directly or indirectly regulates the Mrl1 intracellular trafficking itinerary.
source: This Vrl1-dependent change in Mrl1 distribution suggests that the VINE complex directly or indirectly regulates the Mrl1 intracellular trafficking itinerary.

claim: A Vps10 mutant missing its cytoplasmic tail (Vps10ΔCt) lacks sorting signals and is transported to the vacuolar membrane and lumen.

claim: Expression of VRL1 did not alter the localization of WT Vps10 or Vps10ΔCt.

claim: VINE is required for a subsequent endosome-to-Golgi retrograde transport step for Mrl1.
source: Because VINE is present on budding endosomal tubules and depletes Mrl1 from endosomes, we hypothesize that VINE is required for a subsequent endosome-to-Golgi retrograde transport step.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observed VINE localization and Mrl1 redistribution.

claim: VINE enhances the recycling of the cargo protein Mrl1 at endosomes.
source: Taken together, these results support a model where VINE enhances the recycling of the cargo protein Mrl1 at endosomes (Figure 7L).
evidence: The claim is a summary model based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: Vrl1 is a member of the SNX-BAR protein family.
source: Here, we show that Vrl1 is a member of the SNX-BAR protein family and that it specifically binds the Vps5 paralog Ykr078w/Vin1 to form what we now call the VINE complex.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the structural and functional characterization presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vrl1 specifically binds the Vps5 paralog Ykr078w/Vin1 to form the VINE complex.
source: Here, we show that Vrl1 is a member of the SNX-BAR protein family and that it specifically binds the Vps5 paralog Ykr078w/Vin1 to form what we now call the VINE complex.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the interaction data presented in the manuscript.

claim: VINE is both a VPS9-domain GEF and a SNX-BAR coat complex that may operate alongside the retromer, Mvp1 and Snx4 pathways.
source: Our results suggest that VINE is both a VPS9-domain GEF and a SNX-BAR coat complex that may operate alongside the retromer, Mvp1 and Snx4 pathways.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the functional characterization of VINE.

source: Notably, the human homolog of Vrl1, VARP, physically associates with retromer to drive an endosome-to-plasma membrane sorting pathway (Hesketh et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hesketh et al., 2014.

source: Since common laboratory S. cerevisiae strains carry the non-functional mutant vrl1 allele (Bean et al., 2015)

source: Vrl1 can function as the sole VPS9-domain GEF to stimulate production of endosomal PI3P.

source: Vin1 and Vps5 arose from a single ancestral gene during a whole-genome duplication (WGD) event (Byrne and Wolfe, 2005; Wolfe and Shields, 1997)

source: In pre-WGD species, the single ancestral form of Vps5 must partner with both Vrl1 and Vps17, which requires some promiscuity in BAR-BAR pairing.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the evolutionary history and observed pairing patterns.

claim: The N-termini of the SNX1/Vps5/Vin1 family of SNX-BAR proteins have diversified to bind different proteins and participate in different sorting complexes.
source: Thus, the N-termini of the SNX1/Vps5/Vin1 family of SNX-BAR proteins have diversified to bind different proteins and participate in different sorting complexes.

source: The VINE complex is the first described SNX-BAR coat to possess a VPS9 domain-containing subunit.
